title: Why is Manhattan So Expensive? Regulation and the Rise in Housing Prices
research_question: Why have housing prices in Manhattan and certain other major U.S. metropolitan areas risen so dramatically and remained well above the cost of producing additional housing units? Specifically, to what extent are constraints on new residential supply—rather than demand-side factors—responsible for the persistently high level of housing prices, and can these constraints be justified by negative externalities from new construction?
data_description: The study uses several data sources. Primary price data come from First American Real Estate Corporation condominium sales records for Manhattan, comprising 23,060 transactions from 1984 to 2002, reported per square foot and converted to 2002 dollars. These are supplemented with self-reported values from the New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey (1991–1999) and 1998–99 special metropolitan files of the American Housing Survey covering 21 metropolitan areas (single-family, owner-occupied homes with lot size, square footage, age, and structural characteristics). Construction cost estimates come from R. S. Means, Marshall & Swift, and the NYU Furman Center (Zaxon, Inc.), broken down by building height, quality class, and metropolitan area. Additional inputs include U.S. Census building permits for Manhattan (1955–2000s), CoStar Group commercial office sales data, the 1989 Wharton Land Use Control Survey, and the 1990 Census for 193 cities with populations above 100,000.
institutional_context: Manhattan's housing market is dominated by multi-unit high-rise apartment buildings, where the marginal cost of supplying an additional unit is essentially the cost of adding another floor, and land and site preparation costs are largely fixed. Despite real condominium prices that doubled between the 1980s and early 2000s, new permitting collapsed from roughly 13,000 units in 1960 alone to only 21,000 across the entire 1990s, and newly built structures became shorter on average. Builders face a complex web of land use restrictions, including zoning rules, building codes, the Uniform Land Use Review Process, landmarks preservation requirements, and organized neighborhood opposition (illustrated by episodes like the Battle of Carnegie Hill). Outside Manhattan, other coastal metropolitan areas—particularly in California, the Northeast corridor, and Washington, D.C.—exhibit similarly restrictive permitting environments with long delays between subdivision applications and approvals, while interior heartland cities maintain elastic housing supply.
